moments.title: Turing's 'On Computable Numbers'
moments.body:
A 24-year-old graduate student writes a paper introducing a universal machine that can simulate any other.

In the same paper, Turing proves the halting problem is undecidable; no algorithm can determine in advance whether an arbitrary program will terminate.

quote.text: We may compare a man in the process of computing a real number to a machine which is only capable of a finite number of conditions.

moments.takeaway: The Turing machine became the theoretical foundation of computer science.

moments.title: Von Neumann architecture
moments.body:
The First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC describes a machine where program instructions and data share the same memory.

The stored-program design will dominate computing for decades.
moments.takeaway: A single architectural choice in 1945 shaped almost every subsequent computer.

moments.title: The Manchester Baby runs
moments.body: The Small-Scale Experimental Machine becomes the first stored-program computer to execute a program. It runs for 52 minutes calculating the highest proper factor of a number.
moments.takeaway: Theory met hardware in a university laboratory, not a corporate lab.

now.title: Computing today
now.body: Every computer is, in principle, a Turing machine. The halting problem still has no general solution. New limits (quantum supremacy claims, P vs NP) extend the conversation Turing started.
now.open_questions: Does P equal NP? Can quantum computers solve problems classical computers cannot solve in polynomial time?

items.reflection: Turing was prosecuted for his sexuality in 1952 and died in 1954. How should the history of a field treat the people who built it but were excluded from it?

moments.title: ARPANET sends its first message
moments.body:
On 29 October 1969, Charley Kline tries to log in from UCLA to Stanford. The system crashes after the letters 'L' and 'O'.

The network grows to four nodes by December.
moments.takeaway: The internet's foundational moment was a partial failure.

moments.title: TCP described
moments.body: The paper 'A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication' describes what becomes TCP/IP. The protocol becomes the basis of internetworking.
moments.takeaway: Decoupling networks from their physical layer enabled the open internet.

moments.title: Web proposal at CERN
moments.body: Berners-Lee's March 1989 proposal addresses how to share documents across a heterogeneous research organisation. The first web server runs in 1990.
moments.takeaway: Major shifts can begin as internal solutions to specific organisational problems.

now.title: Networks today
now.body: Roughly 5 billion people now use the internet. Concerns over consolidation, surveillance and resilience shape policy debates around net neutrality and platform regulation.
now.open_questions: How should the internet's open architecture be preserved as more layers concentrate among a few providers?

items.reflection: The internet was built on military funding for academic purposes and then commercialised, with each transition shaping who held power over it.

moments.title: New Directions in Cryptography
moments.who: Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman, Stanford
moments.body: The paper publicly introduces the concept of public-key cryptography, enabling secure communication without prior shared secrets.
moments.takeaway: A theoretical breakthrough made secure communication on open networks possible.

moments.title: RSA published
moments.body: The RSA algorithm provides the first widely deployed public-key system whose security rests on integer factorisation.
moments.takeaway: Mathematical hardness assumptions translated into deployable infrastructure.

moments.title: GCHQ reveals earlier discovery
moments.who: James Ellis, Clifford Cocks and Malcolm Williamson
moments.body: GCHQ discloses that British cryptographers had independently developed analogous public-key methods in the early 1970s, classified at the time.
moments.takeaway: Public scientific history may differ from classified records.

now.title: Cryptography today
now.body: RSA, elliptic-curve and lattice-based methods all underpin internet security. NIST is standardising post-quantum cryptography in anticipation of large-scale quantum computers.
now.open_questions: Will any current public-key algorithm survive practical quantum computing? How is cryptographic agility built into infrastructure?

items.reflection: The same mathematics secures messages and breaks them. Cryptography sits at the intersection of national security and personal privacy.

moments.title: Rosenblatt's perceptron
moments.body:
Rosenblatt's perceptron is the first practical artificial neural network for pattern classification.

Minsky and Papert's 1969 book Perceptrons argues that single-layer networks have fundamental limits, contributing to a first 'AI winter'.
moments.takeaway: Optimism and limit-results have cycled through AI's history.

moments.title: Backpropagation widely adopted
moments.body:
The paper popularises the backpropagation algorithm, allowing efficient training of multi-layer networks.

The method was earlier described by others (Werbos, 1974).
moments.takeaway: Algorithmic improvements without sufficient data and compute can sit unused for decades.

moments.title: AlexNet wins ImageNet
moments.body: AlexNet's deep convolutional network reduces error on the ImageNet competition by a large margin, triggering the modern deep-learning era.
moments.takeaway: The combination of GPUs, large datasets and deep architectures restarted the field.

now.title: AI today
now.body: Large language models and generative systems are deployed across industries. Compute-scaling laws, energy use and governance frameworks are under active debate.
now.open_questions: Will scaling current architectures continue to produce capability gains? How should generative systems be regulated across jurisdictions?

items.reflection: AI's history shows how labels ('intelligent', 'understanding') travel and stretch as the underlying systems change.

moments.title: Babbage describes the Analytical Engine
moments.body: Babbage publishes the first detailed description of his Analytical Engine — a mechanical, general-purpose, programmable computer using punched cards adapted from the Jacquard loom. It would have had a 'store' (memory), 'mill' (CPU), conditional branching, and looping.
moments.takeaway: A general-purpose programmable computer was theoretically described 109 years before the first one ran.

moments.title: Lovelace's notes on the Engine
moments.body: Lovelace translates Luigi Menabrea's French paper on the Analytical Engine and adds 'Notes' three times its length. Note G describes an algorithm to compute Bernoulli numbers — often cited as the first published algorithm intended for a machine. Lovelace also speculates the Engine could compose music or manipulate symbols beyond numbers.

quote.text: The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate anything. It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform.
quote.attrib: Ada Lovelace, Notes on the Analytical Engine, 1843

moments.takeaway: Lovelace grasped that programmability meant the machine was about manipulating symbols, not just calculation.

now.title: Mechanical computing today
now.body: Babbage's Difference Engine No. 2 was finally built by the Science Museum, London, in 1991 (calculating part) and 2002 (printer) — and worked. The Analytical Engine was never built. Ada (the language, 1980) is named for Lovelace; the 'Ada Lovelace Day' second Tuesday of October celebrates women in STEM.
now.open_questions: Why did it take until the 1940s to realise mechanically what Babbage described? Funding, manufacturing tolerances and the absence of a clear market all played roles.

items.reflection: Computing has always had visionaries who saw the destination before the technology existed to take them there. Lovelace's reach beyond pure calculation prefigures the symbolic-AI debates of a century later.

moments.title: An Investigation of the Laws of Thought
moments.body: Boole publishes his second work on symbolic logic. He shows that logical statements can be manipulated algebraically using a small set of operations (AND, OR, NOT) and that this algebra is internally consistent.
moments.takeaway: Reasoning is reduced to algebra — a precondition for electronic computing a century later.

moments.title: Shannon's master's thesis
moments.body: Shannon's master's thesis 'A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits' shows that Boolean algebra can be implemented in electrical relay circuits — the foundation of digital logic design.
moments.takeaway: Boole's algebra and electrical engineering meet, making digital computing physically realisable.

now.title: Boolean logic today
now.body: Every digital circuit, every CPU operation, every database query (WHERE clauses) and every program control flow uses Boolean logic. Shannon's other major work, 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' (1948), founded information theory.
now.open_questions: Are there practical extensions beyond binary? Multi-valued logic, fuzzy logic and quantum computing all explore alternatives — none have replaced two-valued Boolean logic as the substrate of digital systems.

items.reflection: An Irish mathematician working on the foundations of logic in 1854 built the algebraic framework on which all modern computing rests. Pure mathematics often turns out to be applied mathematics on a long lag.

moments.title: A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks
moments.body: Codd publishes his foundational paper in Communications of the ACM, proposing that data should be organised in normalised tables (relations) with no hierarchical or network structure exposed to applications.
moments.takeaway: Decoupling logical data structure from physical storage made databases dramatically more useful and portable.

moments.title: Oracle, IBM DB2 ship relational databases
moments.body: Oracle V2 ships in 1979 as the first commercial relational database. IBM DB2 follows in 1983. By the late 1980s the relational model is dominant in business computing.
moments.takeaway: Theoretical advance translated into commercial product within a decade — driven by the rise of standalone application servers and SQL standardisation (ISO/IEC 9075, 1987).

now.title: Relational databases today
now.body: Relational databases remain the workhorse of business computing. Open-source options (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite) match or exceed commercial systems for many workloads. NoSQL alternatives emerged from 2009 for scale and flexibility but did not replace relational — most large organisations run both.
now.open_questions: How should databases be designed for hybrid transactional/analytical workloads (HTAP)? Cloud-native database architectures (Aurora, Spanner, Snowflake) are redrawing the boundaries.

items.reflection: Codd, who won the 1981 Turing Award, was an academic at heart and disagreed with IBM's eventual SQL implementation (he preferred his own tuple calculus). The product won; the theory was honoured.

moments.title: ARPANET goes live
moments.who: BBN, UCLA, Stanford, UCSB, University of Utah
moments.body: On 29 October 1969, the first ARPANET message is sent between UCLA and Stanford Research Institute. By December 1969 the network has four nodes. The packet-switching design (Paul Baran 1964, Donald Davies 1965) eliminates the single point of failure of circuit-switched networks.
moments.takeaway: A research network funded by the US Department of Defense becomes the technical seed of the global internet.

moments.title: ARPANET adopts TCP/IP
moments.body: On 1 January 1983 ARPANET cuts over from NCP to TCP/IP, making it possible to connect different networks transparently. The cutover ('flag day') was a coordinated effort across all connected systems.
moments.takeaway: Standardising on TCP/IP made internetworking — networks of networks — possible. The internet name dates from this period.

now.title: The internet today
now.body: Around 5 billion people use the internet. The original ARPANET design (open, distributed, end-to-end) has been partly eroded by NAT, CDNs and platform consolidation. ICANN (1998) coordinates names and addresses; the IETF still produces the technical standards.
now.open_questions: How can the open, end-to-end internet architecture be preserved as a few large operators concentrate traffic and DNS?

items.reflection: The decision to publish ARPANET protocols openly, rather than as proprietary military systems, shaped half a century of technology development. Open standards have an outsized effect on long-run outcomes.

moments.title: C is developed at Bell Labs
moments.body: Ritchie develops C as a systems programming language for the PDP-11, derived from B (Ken Thompson) and BCPL. C combines low-level access (pointers, bit operations) with structured-programming constructs.
moments.takeaway: A language designed for writing operating systems became the lingua franca of systems programming for the next 50 years.

moments.title: K&R: The C Programming Language
moments.body: The first edition of 'The C Programming Language' becomes both the de facto language reference and a model for technical writing. The 'Hello, World' program example starts a tradition that survives today.
moments.takeaway: The book sets a standard for concise technical exposition that has influenced programming documentation ever since.

moments.title: ANSI C standard
moments.body: C is formally standardised (C89/C90). The standardisation process resolved ambiguities and made portable C realistic. Later revisions: C99, C11, C17, C23.
moments.takeaway: Standardisation extended C's life and portability for another four decades.

now.title: C today
now.body: C remains foundational: Linux, Windows kernels, embedded systems, databases, language runtimes (CPython, V8). Most other languages compile to or interoperate with C. Memory-safety concerns are gradually pushing systems code toward Rust, but the existing C codebase is enormous and persistent.
now.open_questions: Can the world's installed base of C/C++ systems code be migrated to memory-safe languages? Government agencies (NSA 2022, CISA 2023) have begun publicly recommending this.

items.reflection: Two engineers at Bell Labs built a language that runs almost every operating system you'll ever use, mostly without explicit decision by their employers.

moments.title: Unix begins on a PDP-7
moments.who: Ken Thompson, Dennis Ritchie, Bell Labs
moments.body: After Bell Labs withdraws from the Multics project, Thompson begins a smaller operating system on a spare PDP-7. The first version of Unix supports file system, fork/exec, and a shell.
moments.takeaway: A minor side project replaces the larger system it diverged from.

moments.title: Unix rewritten in C
moments.body: Unix is rewritten in C, making it portable between hardware architectures. This is unusual at a time when operating systems were tied to specific machines.
moments.takeaway: Portability turned Unix from a single-machine project into a transferable platform.

moments.title: BSD and Linux fork the lineage
moments.body: Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) and Linux (kernel 1991, paired with GNU userland) carry the Unix design into open source. macOS (2001) is built on a BSD-derived kernel (Darwin).
moments.takeaway: Open implementations of Unix design now dominate servers, mobile (Android on Linux, iOS on Darwin) and even desktops to some extent.

now.title: Unix philosophy
now.body: 'Write programs that do one thing and do it well; write programs to work together; write programs that handle text streams' (Doug McIlroy) — these principles shape modern Unix systems. Microservices, container architectures and shell pipelines all share intellectual ancestry with early Unix.
now.open_questions: Is the Unix philosophy still applicable to very large-scale distributed systems? Modern cloud architectures combine Unix-style composition with non-Unix orchestration.

items.reflection: Most of the world's computing — almost all servers, all Android phones, all Apple devices — runs systems descended from a 1969 side project at Bell Labs.

moments.title: BASIC at Dartmouth
moments.body: Kemeny and Kurtz design BASIC (Beginner's All-purpose Symbolic Instruction Code) to teach non-STEM students programming on the Dartmouth Time-Sharing System. Simple syntax, line numbers, immediate execution.
moments.takeaway: Programming was designed for beginners deliberately — not all language design defaults to systems programmers.

moments.title: Altair BASIC
moments.who: Bill Gates and Paul Allen, soon to form Microsoft
moments.body: Gates and Allen write Altair BASIC for the MITS Altair 8800 — the first microcomputer to capture hobbyist attention. The product launches Microsoft.
moments.takeaway: Software for personal computers became a business in itself.

moments.title: BBC Micro and home computing
moments.body: BBC Micro (1981) ships with BBC BASIC and becomes the standard in UK schools as part of the BBC Computer Literacy Project. ZX Spectrum (1982), Commodore 64 (1982), Apple II all let users boot into BASIC. A generation of British and American programmers learn on these machines.
moments.takeaway: The BBC Micro alone went into around 80% of UK schools — a deliberate national programme to teach computing.

now.title: Programming for beginners today
now.body: Scratch (MIT, 2007), Python (now the default teaching language), micro:bit (BBC, 2015), the Raspberry Pi (2012) all carry forward the idea that programming should be accessible. The UK's 2014 curriculum reform reintroduced computing as a core subject; BBC's 2015 'Make It Digital' echoed the 1981 initiative.
now.open_questions: Does teaching block-based programming (Scratch) before text-based help or hinder later learning? Empirical evidence is mixed.

items.reflection: BASIC's name reflects an explicit choice: programming was for beginners too. The current resurgence of teaching computing in schools is part of a longer arc whose previous peak was the 1980s home computer boom.

moments.title: Information Management: A Proposal
moments.body: Berners-Lee's March 1989 proposal addresses the loss of information at CERN as researchers come and go. His supervisor Mike Sendall calls it 'vague but exciting' and approves time for prototyping.
moments.takeaway: A proposal that became the foundation of the web was initially described as 'vague but exciting'.

moments.title: First web browser and server
moments.body: By December 1990 Berners-Lee has written the first web browser (WorldWideWeb, on a NeXT machine), the first web server (CERN httpd), and the first web page (info.cern.ch). The HTTP, HTML and URL specifications all date from this work.
moments.takeaway: The web's foundational technologies were built largely by one person in months.

moments.title: CERN releases the web royalty-free
moments.body: On 30 April 1993, CERN puts the underlying technology in the public domain. Mosaic (NCSA, 1993) and then Netscape (1994) bring the web to a mass audience.
moments.takeaway: The decision not to patent or licence the web was decisive in its explosive uptake.

now.title: The web today
now.body: The web is the dominant interface for most computing. HTML, HTTP and URL have all evolved (HTTP/2, HTTP/3 over QUIC; HTML5; URLs extended with WebSockets, ServiceWorkers). The W3C (1994) and WHATWG (2004) coordinate standards. Berners-Lee runs the Solid project (2018) to give users more control over their data.
now.open_questions: Can the web's original decentralisation be restored as platforms concentrate user attention and data?

items.reflection: An internal documentation problem at a physics lab became the most-used application of the internet. The decision to keep the technology open mattered more than any technical choice.

moments.title: Linus announces Linux
moments.body: On 25 August 1991, 21-year-old Torvalds posts to comp.os.minix: 'I'm doing a (free) operating system (just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu) for 386(486) AT clones.' Version 0.01 is released in September; 1.0 follows in 1994.

quote.text: Just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu.

moments.takeaway: An accurate prediction would have been considered grandiose at the time.

moments.title: Open Source Initiative founded
moments.who: Eric Raymond, Bruce Perens and others
moments.body: The Open Source Initiative is founded to promote a business-friendly framing of free software. Netscape releases Mozilla source code the same year. IBM commits to Linux in 1998.
moments.takeaway: Open source moves from movement to industrial strategy as commercial firms adopt it.

now.title: Linux today
now.body: Linux runs essentially all of the world's 500 fastest supercomputers, the majority of web servers, Android (3 billion+ active devices), and substantial fractions of cloud infrastructure. The kernel has had over 22,000 contributors. Linux Foundation hosts not just Linux but Kubernetes, Node.js and many other core projects.
now.open_questions: How sustainable is a model where corporate interests fund most kernel development while individual maintainers remain unpaid?

items.reflection: An undergraduate project in Helsinki became the most widely deployed operating system kernel in history. Open licences and global collaboration made it possible.

moments.title: BackRub at Stanford
moments.who: Larry Page and Sergey Brin, Stanford
moments.body: Page and Brin's PhD project 'BackRub' analyses the link structure of the web. Their PageRank algorithm ranks pages by treating links as votes weighted by the importance of the linking page — a recursive definition with elegant fixed-point properties.
moments.takeaway: Web search before Google was largely keyword matching; the breakthrough was recognising that the link graph itself contained ranking signal.

moments.title: Google incorporated
moments.body: Google is incorporated on 4 September 1998 in a Menlo Park garage. The original investment cheque from Andy Bechtolsheim arrived for Google Inc. before the company existed; it was held for two weeks waiting for incorporation.
moments.takeaway: Algorithmic quality let a search engine win a crowded market within five years (against AltaVista, Excite, Lycos, Yahoo and Microsoft).

now.title: Search today
now.body: Google handles around 9 billion searches per day. PageRank is only one of hundreds of ranking signals. Generative AI (Bing Chat, Google Bard/Gemini, Perplexity) is reshaping the search interface from 'ten blue links' to conversational answers. The economic model — advertising — has remained central since the introduction of AdWords (2000) and AdSense (2003).
now.open_questions: How does search change when answers replace links? Source attribution, monetisation and information quality all need new frameworks.

items.reflection: Two PhD students built the algorithm that organised the web. The financial scale that followed (Alphabet market cap > $2 trillion) is staggering relative to the original computer-science problem.

moments.title: iPhone launch
moments.body: On 9 January 2007 Jobs unveils the iPhone at Macworld. It combines a touchscreen smartphone, iPod and internet device, running OS X. It launches with no SDK for third-party apps — Jobs initially preferred web apps.
moments.takeaway: The smartphone existed before the iPhone (BlackBerry, Windows Mobile, Symbian); the iPhone redefined what it was.

moments.title: App Store opens
moments.body: On 10 July 2008 the App Store launches with 500 apps. By 2024 there were over 1.8 million apps. The 30%/15% revenue share model becomes the basis of platform economics for the next decade.
moments.takeaway: App stores turned smartphones into developer platforms with a controlled distribution channel.

moments.title: Android and the open alternative
moments.body: HTC Dream (T-Mobile G1) ships with Android in October 2008. Android's open licensing — installed by many manufacturers (Samsung, Xiaomi, Huawei) — eventually gives it the majority of global smartphone market share.
moments.takeaway: Two distinct strategies (closed integrated vs open licensed) co-exist; the platform/handset bifurcation echoes the 1980s PC/Mac split.

now.title: Mobile-first today
now.body: Around 7 billion smartphones globally; ~85% of internet users access via mobile. App stores have come under regulatory pressure (EU Digital Markets Act 2022 forces app store competition on iOS in 2024). Mobile shaped UI conventions, network protocols (mobile-optimised HTTP), photography and payment systems.
now.open_questions: What is the next major form factor? AR/VR (Apple Vision Pro 2024, Meta Quest), wearables and voice interfaces compete; none has yet replaced the smartphone.

items.reflection: A single product launch in 2007 redefined consumer computing for at least the next two decades. Platform decisions made at launch (App Store rules, hardware integration) still shape how digital industries operate.

moments.title: Hollerith tabulators run the US census
moments.body: The 1880 census took eight years to process; Hollerith's electromechanical tabulator processes the 1890 census in roughly one year. Cards encode demographic data as patterns of holes; electric pins close circuits where holes exist, advancing counters.
moments.takeaway: Data processing became a mechanised industry decades before electronic computing — and the company Hollerith founded became IBM in 1924.

moments.title: The 80-column IBM card
moments.body: IBM standardises the 80-column rectangular-hole punched card. It will dominate business data processing for fifty years. The 80-column line length still persists in terminal width conventions and many programming style guides.
moments.takeaway: Industrial standards from the mechanical era shape software conventions a century later.

now.title: Data processing today
now.body: Punched cards disappeared by the 1980s but the conceptual lineage runs straight to relational databases and column-oriented data warehouses. The phrase 'do not fold, spindle or mutilate' (a 1960s card-handling instruction) became a slogan of 1960s student protest against bureaucratisation.
now.open_questions: How do legacy systems written for 80-column data still constrain modern data pipelines? COBOL systems running mainframe financial workloads are an active question.

items.reflection: Hollerith's machines were used by the US census but also, in their European subsidiary Dehomag, by Nazi Germany to organise the 1933 and 1939 census data used in the Holocaust. The history of data processing is inseparable from the history of state power.

moments.title: Church's lambda calculus and the Church-Turing thesis
moments.body: Church publishes 'An Unsolvable Problem of Elementary Number Theory', using lambda calculus to give a different but equivalent definition of effective computability. Turing demonstrates the equivalence in his 1936 paper.
moments.takeaway: Two completely different formalisms — lambda calculus and Turing machines — define exactly the same set of computable functions. This is the Church-Turing thesis.

now.title: Functional programming today
now.body: Lambda calculus is the direct ancestor of LISP, Haskell, ML, F#, Scala, and the functional features added to JavaScript, Python and Java. The 2010s adoption of map/filter/reduce in mainstream languages is a delayed mainstreaming of 1936 mathematics.
now.open_questions: Is the Church-Turing thesis fundamentally a statement about physics or about mathematics? Quantum computing extends it (BQP rather than P), but does not violate it.

items.reflection: Turing was Church's PhD student at Princeton in 1936-38. The relationship between supervisor and student produced two of the foundational papers of computer science within months.

moments.title: Bletchley Park breaks Enigma
moments.who: Alan Turing, Gordon Welchman, Joan Clarke and ~10,000 others
moments.body: The Government Code and Cypher School moves to Bletchley Park in August 1939. Polish mathematicians (Rejewski, Zygalski, Rozycki) had already broken early Enigma in 1932; their work is handed to British and French allies in July 1939. Turing and Welchman design the Bombe electromechanical machine to test possible Enigma settings.
moments.takeaway: Industrial-scale codebreaking, classified for thirty years after the war, shaped both the development of computing and Allied victory.

moments.title: Colossus runs at Bletchley
moments.who: Tommy Flowers, Post Office Research Station
moments.body: Flowers' Colossus, used to attack the Lorenz cipher (used by Hitler and the German High Command), uses 1,500 vacuum tubes — and Colossus 2 (June 1944) uses 2,400. It is the first programmable, electronic, digital computing device. All ten Colossus machines were destroyed after the war to keep them secret.
moments.takeaway: The first electronic computers were built for war, not commerce — and the destruction of the machines erased credit for British computing pioneers for decades.

now.title: Codebreaking today
now.body: GCHQ (the postwar successor to Bletchley) remains the UK's signals intelligence agency. The codebreaking work was declassified gradually from 1974 (F.W. Winterbotham's The Ultra Secret) onwards. The Bletchley Park site is now a museum; the National Museum of Computing on the same site holds a working Colossus rebuild.
now.open_questions: How much did Bletchley shorten the war? Estimates range from 18 months to four years — and from 14 to 21 million lives saved.

items.reflection: Many of Bletchley's 10,000 staff were women (approx. 75%), working as cryptanalysts, linguists and Bombe operators. Their work was kept secret from their families for decades. Joan Clarke, Turing's close colleague and briefly fiancee, did not receive public recognition until long after her death in 1996.

moments.title: ENIAC unveiled
moments.who: John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert, University of Pennsylvania
moments.body: The Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer is unveiled on 14 February 1946. It weighs 30 tons, uses 17,468 vacuum tubes and consumes 150 kW. It was commissioned by the US Army for artillery firing tables. Six women — Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Fran Bilas and Ruth Lichterman — were its original programmers, hired as 'computers' (a job title for human calculators).
moments.takeaway: The first general-purpose electronic computer was programmed by women whose names were absent from public coverage for decades.

now.title: Programmers today
now.body: The six ENIAC programmers were inducted into the Women in Technology International Hall of Fame in 1997 — 50 years late. Their story (Kathy Kleiman's research and the 2014 documentary 'The Computers') reshaped popular understanding of computing's origins.
now.open_questions: Why did programming, originally a female-coded job, become male-coded between 1950 and 1990? Mar Hicks' 'Programmed Inequality' (2017) traces the UK's deliberate exclusion of women from computing careers from the 1960s.

items.reflection: Software was originally seen as clerical work — repetitive, detail-focused, suitable for women — while hardware was 'real' engineering. The status reversal as programming became prestigious tracks the gender flip.

moments.title: FORTRAN released
moments.body: After three years of work, IBM releases FORTRAN (Formula Translation) for the IBM 704. Backus's team had to convince sceptical engineers that a compiler could produce machine code as efficient as hand-written assembly. They largely succeeded — and the productivity gain was overwhelming.
moments.takeaway: The first major high-level language proved that programmers did not need to think in machine code. Productivity rather than efficiency drove the abstraction.

moments.title: COBOL designed
moments.body: Hopper, a US Navy commander and PhD mathematician, had built FLOW-MATIC (1955), the first English-like programming language. COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language) builds on it. Hopper's insight: business code should read like English so non-programmers could verify what it did.

quote.text: It's easier to ask forgiveness than it is to get permission.

moments.takeaway: Hopper's COBOL became the language of business computing for sixty years. An estimated 200+ billion lines of COBOL are still running in 2024 — mostly in banks, insurance and government.

now.title: Languages today
now.body: FORTRAN remains in scientific high-performance computing (climate models, computational fluid dynamics). COBOL runs ~70% of global business transaction volume by some estimates. Hopper is buried with full military honours at Arlington; the USS Hopper destroyer is named for her.
now.open_questions: How long will COBOL persist? US state unemployment systems collapsed during COVID-19 partly because COBOL maintainers had retired.

items.reflection: Hopper also coined 'debugging' after finding an actual moth in a relay of the Harvard Mark II (1947). The log entry — with the moth taped in — is preserved at the Smithsonian.

moments.title: John McCarthy designs LISP
moments.body: McCarthy (who also coined 'artificial intelligence' in 1956) designs LISP (LISt Processor) as a programming language for AI research. Its homoiconic syntax (code is data) and treatment of functions as first-class values were extraordinary for 1958. The eval/apply core of LISP is described in seven primitive operations.
moments.takeaway: LISP's design ideas (garbage collection, dynamic typing, REPL, recursion, higher-order functions) took decades to reach mainstream languages — but all reached them eventually.

now.title: LISP today
now.body: Clojure (2007, Rich Hickey), Scheme, Common Lisp and Racket continue the family. Emacs (1976) is largely Emacs Lisp. JavaScript's first-class functions are a LISP inheritance via Brendan Eich's design. Paul Graham's essays argue LISP gave his startup Viaweb decisive advantages over competitors in the 1990s.
now.open_questions: Why hasn't LISP itself become mainstream despite its ideas dominating language design?

items.reflection: McCarthy designed LISP on paper for theoretical purposes; his graduate student Steve Russell implemented eval in machine code without asking permission, and LISP existed. Sometimes the implementer matters more than the designer.

moments.title: Dijkstra's algorithm
moments.body: Dijkstra, then 26, designs his shortest-path algorithm in roughly 20 minutes while having coffee with his fiancee in an Amsterdam cafe. He needed a problem demonstrable to non-specialists to show the power of the new ARMAC computer. He chose the shortest route between two Dutch cities.
moments.takeaway: One of the most-used algorithms in routing, networking and AI search was devised in twenty minutes without paper or pencil — and not published for three years because Dijkstra thought it too trivial.

moments.title: 'Go To Statement Considered Harmful'
moments.body: Dijkstra's letter to Communications of the ACM (titled by editor Niklaus Wirth) argues that goto-based control flow makes programs hard to reason about. The letter triggers the structured programming movement and shapes language design (Pascal, Modula, C).

quote.text: The quality of programmers is a decreasing function of the density of go to statements in the programs they produce.

moments.takeaway: A 1968 polemic by a single computer scientist reshaped how programmers wrote code for decades.

now.title: Algorithms today
now.body: Dijkstra's algorithm runs every time your phone calculates a route. Google Maps, OpenStreetMap, IP routing protocols (OSPF, IS-IS), network packet routing — all variations. The structured programming movement gave us if/while/for and the elimination of goto from most modern languages.
now.open_questions: Does Dijkstra's elegance bias us against messy but effective heuristics? Modern routing combines exact algorithms with learned heuristics (A*, contraction hierarchies).

items.reflection: Dijkstra wrote his papers by hand and gave them numbers (EWD1 through EWD1318). The 'EWD' archive is still hosted at UT Austin where he taught from 1984. He believed computer science had been corrupted by IBM marketing.

moments.title: Volume 1 of The Art of Computer Programming
moments.body: Knuth begins TAOCP in 1962 as a single volume on compilers. By 1968 Volume 1 alone is published. The series is projected to be seven volumes; four and parts of a fifth have appeared by 2024. Bill Gates: 'If you think you're a really good programmer... read [Knuth's] Art of Computer Programming. You should definitely send me a resume if you can read the whole thing.'
moments.takeaway: The standard reference work on algorithms has been a lifetime project. Knuth pays $2.56 for each error found (a hexadecimal dollar).

moments.title: Knuth creates TeX
moments.body: Frustrated with the typography of TAOCP's reprint, Knuth designs TeX, a typesetting system. He intends to take a year. He takes ten. TeX has not had a bug since 2008; its version number asymptotically approaches pi.
moments.takeaway: Almost all scientific papers (LaTeX is built on TeX) are typeset with software written because one author wanted his books to look right.

now.title: Algorithm analysis today
now.body: Big-O notation (Knuth popularised it), worst-case analysis, amortised analysis — all standard CS education. CLRS (Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein) succeeded TAOCP as the standard teaching text in the 1990s. Knuth retired from teaching in 1992 'to finish TAOCP'.
now.open_questions: Are there fundamental algorithm classes still to be discovered? Or are we down to constant-factor improvements?

items.reflection: Knuth has not used email since 1990. He receives faxes monthly. He believes deep thinking requires uninterrupted attention. This stance is increasingly extreme — and increasingly imitated.

moments.title: Smalltalk at PARC
moments.who: Alan Kay, Dan Ingalls, Adele Goldberg, Xerox PARC
moments.body: Kay's team at Xerox PARC develops Smalltalk, the first fully object-oriented language. Everything is an object; everything communicates by sending messages. The Alto workstation that ran Smalltalk also pioneered the bitmap display, mouse, GUI, WYSIWYG editing and Ethernet — all in 1973.
moments.takeaway: Almost every interface element on every screen you've ever used was prototyped at Xerox PARC by 1975. Xerox failed to commercialise any of it.

moments.title: Steve Jobs visits PARC
moments.body: Jobs and a small Apple team are shown the Xerox Alto in a famous December 1979 visit. They focus on the GUI; they miss object-oriented programming, the network and SmallTalk's deep ideas. The Lisa (1983) and Macintosh (1984) borrow the GUI; Microsoft borrows from the Mac.

quote.text: Good artists copy, great artists steal.
quote.attrib: Steve Jobs, attributed (he attributed it to Picasso)

moments.takeaway: The most influential computer demo in history transferred ideas from a research lab that could not productise them to a startup that could.

now.title: OOP today
now.body: Object-oriented programming dominated language design from C++ (1979) and Java (1995) through the 2000s. Functional programming has reasserted itself (Scala, Kotlin, Rust traits, JavaScript). 'Composition over inheritance' is now mainstream advice. Kay has long argued real OOP — messages between objects — has not been widely understood.
now.open_questions: Does the next interface paradigm exist somewhere already, prototyped and unrecognised?

items.reflection: Alan Kay's 1972 vision of the 'Dynabook' — a personal, networked, tablet-sized computer for children — directly anticipated the iPad (2010, by 38 years). Kay was at Apple at the time but the iPad team did not consult him.

moments.title: Moore's Law published
moments.body: In Electronics magazine, Moore (then at Fairchild Semiconductor) predicts the number of transistors per integrated circuit will double approximately every year. He revises to every two years in 1975. The prediction held for roughly 50 years before slowing in the 2010s.
moments.takeaway: A trend article in a trade magazine became the organising principle of an industry — partly because the industry organised to make it true.

moments.title: Intel 4004
moments.who: Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor, Masatoshi Shima, Intel
moments.body: The Intel 4004 ships in November 1971. It's the first commercially available microprocessor: a complete CPU on a single chip. 2,300 transistors, 740 kHz, designed for a Japanese calculator (the Busicom 141-PF). The deal terms allowed Intel to sell it for non-calculator uses.
moments.takeaway: The microprocessor was a calculator part. Its general-purpose use was a side-bet that became the entire industry.

now.title: Chips today
now.body: A 2024 high-end mobile SoC (Apple A18 Pro) has 20+ billion transistors at ~3nm. Moore's Law is widely declared dead but performance still scales (chiplets, 3D stacking, specialisation: GPUs, NPUs). TSMC fabricates the leading-edge chips for almost all major customers; the US CHIPS Act (2022) is a $52bn attempt to reshore manufacturing.
now.open_questions: How long can transistor scaling continue? Quantum effects, heat dissipation and lithography are all near physical limits.

items.reflection: Three of the 4004's designers were Italian, Japanese, Polish and American. Faggin (Italian-American) had to fight to get his name etched on the chip's mask. Silicon Valley has always been more international than its marketing suggests.

moments.title: Altair 8800 on the cover of Popular Electronics
moments.body: The January 1975 cover features the Altair 8800 microcomputer kit ($397 assembled, $439 with case). MITS expects to sell 200; they sell thousands. There is no keyboard, no screen — toggle switches and blinking lights. The Homebrew Computer Club forms in Menlo Park in March to share information about it.
moments.takeaway: The personal computer began as a hobbyist kit with no software. It existed for the joy of having one.

moments.title: Apple I
moments.body: Wozniak designs the Apple I single-board computer; Jobs sells his VW van and Wozniak sells his HP-65 calculator to start production. They sell about 200 (around $666.66 each). The Apple II (April 1977) brings colour graphics, sound and the BASIC interpreter — and becomes the first mass-market personal computer.
moments.takeaway: Apple began as a Homebrew Computer Club project. Wozniak's hardware genius and Jobs' relentless commercialisation were both required.

moments.title: IBM PC
moments.who: IBM, Don Estridge's Boca Raton team
moments.body: IBM ships the 5150 PC on 12 August 1981. The team decides — under time pressure — to use off-the-shelf parts and licence DOS from a tiny company called Microsoft. IBM does not lock down the architecture. Within a year, Compaq has shipped a clone. IBM never recovers control of the PC market.
moments.takeaway: IBM's decision to use open architecture created a $1 trillion ecosystem and destroyed IBM's PC business.

now.title: Personal computing today
now.body: The PC market is mature (~270 million units a year). Apple's M1/M2/M3/M4 chips (2020-onwards) shifted Macs from Intel to ARM, ending the WinTel duopoly that defined the 1990s-2000s. Chromebooks, tablets and smartphones all eat into traditional PC use.
now.open_questions: Is the desktop/laptop still the productivity computer in 2034? Mobile-first generations work differently.

items.reflection: Bill Gates was 19 and Steve Jobs was 21 in 1975-76. The entire industry was created by people under 25. Most subsequent computing industries (Facebook, Google, Snapchat, OpenAI) were founded by people in their 20s.

moments.title: Macintosh launch and the '1984' ad
moments.body: The 1984 Super Bowl ad (directed by Ridley Scott) costs $370,000 and airs once. The Macintosh launches on 24 January 1984 with a $2,495 price tag, MacWrite, MacPaint and a mouse. It's the first mass-market computer with a GUI built in. Jobs reveals it by pulling it from a bag and letting it introduce itself in synthesised speech.
moments.takeaway: The Mac put a graphical interface into millions of homes — and made advertising central to tech product launches.

moments.title: Windows 1.0
moments.body: Microsoft Windows 1.0 ships on 20 November 1985 after multiple delays. It's a graphical shell over MS-DOS. Windows 3.0 (1990) and 3.1 (1992) make Windows the dominant GUI. Windows 95 (24 August 1995) integrates the GUI and adds a Start menu, taskbar and Internet Explorer.
moments.takeaway: Microsoft caught the GUI wave by being persistent rather than first. Windows shipped six years after the Mac but on far more hardware.

now.title: Interfaces today
now.body: WIMP (Windows, Icons, Menus, Pointer) interfaces remain dominant for productivity work. Touch (smartphones, tablets), voice (Alexa, Siri), and chat (ChatGPT) are the major alternatives. The Mac and Windows are 40+ years old, and still essentially recognisable to their first users.
now.open_questions: Is generative AI replacing GUIs with conversation? Or augmenting them? OpenAI's GPT-powered computer-use agents (2024-) suggest the latter.

items.reflection: The Macintosh team called themselves 'pirates' and flew a skull-and-crossbones over their building. The Microsoft team copied their work. The story of the GUI is the story of who finished and shipped.

moments.title: Ethernet sketched at PARC
moments.who: Robert Metcalfe and David Boggs, Xerox PARC
moments.body: Metcalfe's 22 May 1973 memo describes a system inspired by the ALOHAnet (University of Hawaii, 1971): computers share a single cable, detect collisions, and retry after random delays (CSMA/CD). Initially named 'Alto Aloha Network', then renamed 'Ethernet' after the 19th-century luminiferous ether.
moments.takeaway: A network designed for one building became the standard for local-area networking worldwide.

moments.title: DIX standard (DEC, Intel, Xerox)
moments.body: Ethernet is published as a multi-vendor standard. IEEE 802.3 follows in 1983. Ethernet beats Token Ring (IBM) and ARCnet by being cheaper, faster and more permissive.
moments.takeaway: Open standards beat closed competitors even when the closed competitors had IBM behind them.

now.title: Networking today
now.body: Ethernet runs at 1 Gbps standard, 10/40/100/400 Gbps in data centres. Wi-Fi (802.11, 1997) is wireless Ethernet's grandchild. The Ethernet frame format is essentially unchanged since 1980 — a remarkable example of stable infrastructure.
now.open_questions: Will optical interconnects replace electrical Ethernet at short range? Co-packaged optics are emerging at 800Gbps.

items.reflection: Metcalfe left Xerox in 1979 and founded 3Com to sell Ethernet adapters. He coined Metcalfe's Law (network value scales as n²) and was awarded the 2022 Turing Award. Xerox PARC produced the ideas; others built the businesses.

moments.title: The Morris Worm
moments.body: On 2 November 1988, Morris (a Cornell graduate student, son of an NSA chief scientist) releases a self-propagating program that exploits sendmail, finger and rsh vulnerabilities. A coding bug makes it propagate far faster than intended; it infects ~10% of the internet (around 6,000 of 60,000 connected machines). Morris is the first person convicted under the 1986 Computer Fraud and Abuse Act.
moments.takeaway: The first major internet security incident was a student experiment that escaped containment. It triggered the creation of CERT (Computer Emergency Response Team) at Carnegie Mellon.

moments.title: Stuxnet revealed
moments.body: Stuxnet, discovered in 2010 but operational from 2007, targets Siemens PLCs controlling centrifuges at Iran's Natanz uranium enrichment facility. It causes ~1,000 centrifuges to spin to destruction while reporting normal operation. The attribution to the US and Israel is now public.
moments.takeaway: Stuxnet was the first known act of digital sabotage causing physical destruction by a nation-state. It changed the perceived stakes of cybersecurity.

moments.title: WannaCry ransomware
moments.body: On 12 May 2017, WannaCry ransomware encrypts files on hundreds of thousands of Windows computers in 150 countries, demanding Bitcoin payment. The UK's NHS is severely affected; some hospitals turn patients away. It exploits EternalBlue, an NSA tool leaked weeks earlier by the Shadow Brokers. Marcus Hutchins ('MalwareTech') accidentally activates a killswitch by registering a domain in the malware.
moments.takeaway: Government cyber-weapons leaked into criminal hands disabled hospitals across the world within months.

now.title: Cybersecurity today
now.body: Ransomware extracted billions in 2023. The SolarWinds breach (2020) and Log4Shell (2021) showed how supply-chain attacks scale. Critical infrastructure attacks (Colonial Pipeline 2021, Ukrainian power grid 2015 and 2016) are now routine. NIST, NCSC and ENISA coordinate national cybersecurity standards.
now.open_questions: Can software liability law shift from disclaimers ('AS IS') to manufacturer responsibility? The 2023 US National Cybersecurity Strategy proposes this.

items.reflection: Morris was sentenced to community service and a $10,050 fine; he later became an MIT professor and co-founded Y Combinator. The boundary between security research, mischief and crime is set by intent and consequence, not by code.

moments.title: Wikipedia launches
moments.body: Wikipedia goes live on 15 January 2001 as a side project to Nupedia, an expert-only encyclopedia. The wiki version (built on Ward Cunningham's 1995 WikiWikiWeb concept) immediately produces more content. By end of 2001 there are 20,000 articles; by 2024, 60+ million across 300+ languages.
moments.takeaway: An open, anyone-can-edit encyclopedia became more comprehensive and at least as accurate as Britannica (Nature 2005 study) within five years.

moments.title: Web 2.0 era
moments.who: Mark Zuckerberg, Steve Chen, Jack Dorsey and others
moments.body: Facebook (Feb 2004), YouTube (Feb 2005, sold to Google Nov 2006 for $1.65bn), Twitter (March 2006), Reddit (June 2005). The 'Web 2.0' conference (2004) names the shift to user-generated content, AJAX-driven dynamic interfaces, and social networking.
moments.takeaway: The web's second generation moved value from publishing to interaction. The economic model shifted from selling content to monetising attention.

now.title: Open knowledge today
now.body: Wikipedia is the eighth-most-visited site globally. It is increasingly the training corpus for LLMs — which now answer questions Wikipedia used to. Twitter/X, Facebook and YouTube have all undergone significant changes (acquisition, regulatory scrutiny). Mastodon and Bluesky offer decentralised alternatives.
now.open_questions: If LLMs replace Wikipedia for answers, who edits the underlying knowledge? Volunteer editor numbers are falling.

items.reflection: Wikipedia runs on around $180m annually — about 0.001% of the revenue of platforms that ingest its content. The 'free' web is funded by a tiny fraction of the value it creates.

moments.title: Deep Blue defeats Kasparov
moments.body: On 11 May 1997, IBM's Deep Blue defeats world chess champion Garry Kasparov 3.5-2.5 in a six-game match in New York. Deep Blue evaluates ~200 million chess positions per second using custom hardware and brute-force search with handcrafted evaluation functions. Kasparov accuses IBM of human intervention; IBM dismantles the machine and refuses a rematch.
moments.takeaway: Chess fell to specialised hardware and search. The result was widely treated as the AI 'winning' — though Deep Blue understood nothing.

moments.title: AlphaGo defeats Lee Sedol
moments.body: In March 2016 in Seoul, DeepMind's AlphaGo defeats 18-time world Go champion Lee Sedol 4-1. Go has ~10^170 possible board positions (more than atoms in the observable universe), making brute force impossible. AlphaGo uses deep neural networks trained on human games plus self-play, with Monte Carlo Tree Search. Move 37 of Game 2 — a play no human would make — is now famous.

quote.text: I thought AlphaGo was based on probability calculation and it was merely a machine. But when I saw this move, I changed my mind. Surely AlphaGo is creative.

moments.takeaway: Go required learning, not search. The methods that solved it became the methods of the deep-learning era.

moments.title: ChatGPT released
moments.body: ChatGPT launches on 30 November 2022 as a research preview. It reaches 1 million users in 5 days, 100 million in 2 months — the fastest-growing consumer app in history. GPT-4 follows in March 2023. The release moves large language models from research to everyday tool.
moments.takeaway: Generative AI became mainstream not through a research breakthrough but through a chat interface wrapped around an existing model (GPT-3.5).

now.title: AI today
now.body: Frontier labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta AI, xAI) compete on model capability. The EU AI Act (2024), US Executive Order (2023, revoked 2025), and UK AI Safety Institute represent emerging governance. Compute requirements and energy use are major constraints.
now.open_questions: Will continued scaling produce general intelligence, or hit fundamental limits? Are LLMs reasoning or pattern-matching?

items.reflection: Lee Sedol retired from professional Go in 2019, citing 'an entity that cannot be defeated'. He played his last professional match against Korean AI HanDol — and won. The relationship between humans and superhuman systems is still being worked out, one game at a time.

moments.title: Amazon Web Services launches
moments.body: S3 (Simple Storage Service) launches on 14 March 2006; EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) follows in August. Amazon — an online bookstore — sells excess computing capacity built for its retail traffic. CEO Jeff Bezos backs the strategy despite scepticism. By 2024 AWS generates ~$100bn in annual revenue at ~30% operating margin.
moments.takeaway: Cloud computing turned servers from capital expenditure into operating expenditure. Startups no longer needed to buy hardware to launch.

moments.title: Azure and Google Cloud arrive
moments.body: Microsoft Azure launches in February 2010; Google Compute Engine in 2013 (though App Engine existed from 2008). The 'big three' clouds (AWS, Azure, GCP) take ~65% of the cloud infrastructure market by 2024.
moments.takeaway: Cloud became infrastructure on which competitors of the cloud provider build their businesses. Netflix runs on AWS while competing with Amazon Prime Video.

now.title: Cloud today
now.body: Most new software is cloud-native. Kubernetes (Google, 2014, open-sourced 2015) is the standard container orchestration. Serverless (AWS Lambda, 2014) abstracts away machines entirely. AI workloads are reshaping cloud economics: Nvidia GPUs are scarce, expensive and central.
now.open_questions: Does cloud concentration create geopolitical and economic risks? Sovereign cloud initiatives (EU, India, China) reflect concern.

items.reflection: Bezos' insistence that every Amazon team expose its work via APIs (the 2002 'Bezos mandate') accidentally laid the groundwork for AWS. Internal architecture became external product.

moments.title: Cook's theorem
moments.body: Cook proves the Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT) is NP-complete: every problem in NP can be reduced to SAT in polynomial time. This defines a class of problems that all rise or fall together — solve one efficiently, solve them all.
moments.takeaway: Computer science gained a tool for proving problems hard without proving them impossible.

moments.title: Karp's 21 NP-complete problems
moments.body: Karp's paper 'Reducibility Among Combinatorial Problems' shows 21 well-known problems are NP-complete: travelling salesman, graph colouring, knapsack, Hamiltonian cycle, vertex cover. Within a few years hundreds of NP-complete problems are catalogued (Garey and Johnson, 1979).
moments.takeaway: The NP-complete class explained why so many practically important problems seemed to resist efficient solution.

now.title: Complexity today
now.body: P vs NP remains the most famous open problem in computer science. The Clay Mathematics Institute offers $1 million for a solution; it is one of seven Millennium Prize problems. Most researchers believe P ≠ NP. Modern cryptography would collapse if P = NP.
now.open_questions: Does P equal NP? Quantum complexity (BQP) adds new classes. Average-case complexity matters more than worst-case for practical algorithms.

items.reflection: Donald Knuth offered to pay $0.32 for any answer to P vs NP — a hexadecimal pound — but specified he was betting on P = NP. He has lost no money so far.

moments.title: Python 0.9.0
moments.body: Van Rossum releases Python 0.9.0 in February 1991. Named after Monty Python's Flying Circus, not the snake. He designed it during a Christmas holiday as a successor to ABC (a teaching language) with better support for system programming. Indentation-based syntax forces readable code.
moments.takeaway: Python's design priorities — readability, batteries-included, one obvious way — built a language that beginners and professionals could share.

moments.title: Python 3 released
moments.body: Python 3.0 ships on 3 December 2008, deliberately breaking backward compatibility (mainly to fix Unicode and division). The migration takes a decade; Python 2 reaches end-of-life on 1 January 2020.
moments.takeaway: Even popular languages can take ten years to migrate users between incompatible versions.

now.title: Python today
now.body: Python is the most popular programming language by most measures (TIOBE, RedMonk, PYPL). It dominates data science (NumPy, pandas), machine learning (PyTorch, TensorFlow), and education. PEP 8 style and the Zen of Python (PEP 20) shape how Python feels. The Steering Council (since 2019) governs the language after van Rossum stepped down.
now.open_questions: Can Python's performance keep up? PyPy, Mojo and Python 3.12+ optimisations (no-GIL Python from 3.13) attempt to address it.

items.reflection: Van Rossum's title was 'Benevolent Dictator For Life' until he resigned in 2018 over disputes about adding the walrus operator (:=). Language design at scale needs governance, not just designers.

moments.title: Java 1.0
moments.body: Gosling's team at Sun designs Java (originally 'Oak') from 1991 for set-top boxes. The project pivots to the web in 1995, with applets running in browsers. The Java promise: 'Write once, run anywhere' — the JVM abstracts hardware. Java 1.0 ships in January 1996.
moments.takeaway: Java's bytecode/JVM design separated language from platform — an idea that influences .NET, JavaScript engines and WebAssembly.

moments.title: Oracle acquires Sun
moments.body: Oracle's $7.4 billion acquisition gives it Java, MySQL, Solaris and Sun's hardware business. Subsequent lawsuits (Oracle v. Google over Android's use of Java APIs, 2010-2021) shape software copyright law. The Supreme Court eventually rules for Google (fair use, 2021).
moments.takeaway: A 2009 acquisition triggered a decade-long lawsuit that defined whether APIs are copyrightable. The answer (essentially: no, when reuse is transformative) shaped open ecosystems.

now.title: Java today
now.body: Java runs ~9 billion devices. The JVM hosts Kotlin (Android's primary language since 2017), Scala, Clojure and JRuby. Modern Java (versions 17 LTS, 21 LTS) is closer to functional languages than 1990s Java was. Enterprise back-ends remain heavily Java; banks run trillions of dollars on JVM applications.
now.open_questions: Will GraalVM, Project Loom (virtual threads) and Valhalla (value types) keep Java performance-competitive with newer languages?

items.reflection: The 'duke' mascot and the coffee-cup logo are 1995 cultural artefacts. Java's name came from Peet's coffee in Berkeley. Engineers name their work after their habits.

moments.title: Linus Torvalds writes Git
moments.body: After BitKeeper revokes its free licence for Linux kernel use, Torvalds writes Git in two weeks (3 April 2005 start). 'I'm an egotistical bastard, and I name all my projects after myself. First Linux, now Git.' (Git: British slang for an unpleasant person.) Distributed model: every clone is a full repository.
moments.takeaway: Distributed version control made open-source collaboration scale. Centralised systems (SVN, CVS) faded within a decade.

moments.title: GitHub launches
moments.who: Tom Preston-Werner, Chris Wanstrath, P. J. Hyett
moments.body: GitHub launches in April 2008, hosting Git repositories with social features (fork, pull request, profile). It becomes the dominant code-hosting platform within five years. Microsoft acquires GitHub in 2018 for $7.5 billion.
moments.takeaway: GitHub turned open source from project-by-project to a unified social graph of code. The pull request — a UI invention — reshaped how software is reviewed.

now.title: Version control today
now.body: Git is essentially universal. GitHub Copilot (2021) and similar AI tools generate code from comments. GitHub hosts 400+ million repositories and 100+ million developers. Alternatives (GitLab, Bitbucket, Forgejo) compete on price and features.
now.open_questions: How does AI-generated code change attribution, licensing and code review? The lawsuits are starting.

items.reflection: Torvalds wrote Linux in 1991 and Git in 2005. Two of the most-used pieces of software in the world come from the same person. He still manages the Linux kernel from a home office in Portland, Oregon.

moments.title: Brewer's CAP theorem
moments.body: Brewer's PODC keynote conjectures that distributed systems cannot simultaneously provide Consistency, Availability and Partition tolerance — only two of three. Gilbert and Lynch prove it in 2002. The result reshapes how distributed databases are designed.
moments.takeaway: A theoretical impossibility result became a daily practical concern for every team building distributed systems.

moments.title: NoSQL era
moments.body: Google's Bigtable paper (2006), Amazon's Dynamo paper (2007), and open-source implementations — MongoDB (2009), Cassandra (2008 from Facebook), Redis (2009), CouchDB (2005) — reject the relational model for web-scale workloads. 'NoSQL' is coined at a 2009 San Francisco meetup.
moments.takeaway: Web-scale requirements drove databases to abandon ACID for eventual consistency. The pendulum has since swung back (NewSQL, Spanner).

now.title: Databases today
now.body: Most large architectures use multiple databases: relational for transactions, NoSQL for scale, vector databases for AI, time-series for telemetry, graph for social networks. Cloud-managed databases (RDS, Aurora, Cosmos DB, Spanner) abstract operations.
now.open_questions: Are vector databases (Pinecone, Weaviate, pgvector) a lasting category or a feature of existing databases?

items.reflection: Brewer (a Berkeley professor and Inktomi co-founder) joined Google as VP of Infrastructure. The theoretical and practical sides of databases keep colliding in the same career.

moments.title: Snowden disclosures
moments.body: From 5 June 2013, the Guardian and Washington Post publish stories based on documents Snowden gave to journalists Glenn Greenwald, Laura Poitras and Bart Gellman. The PRISM program collects data from Google, Facebook, Apple and others; XKeyscore enables analyst queries across global internet traffic. Snowden flees to Hong Kong then Moscow.
moments.takeaway: Mass surveillance of internet traffic and metadata, long suspected, was documented in primary sources. The post-Snowden internet is more encrypted by default.

now.title: Privacy today
now.body: HTTPS is now near-universal (Let's Encrypt, 2016, drove uptake). End-to-end encrypted messaging (Signal, WhatsApp) is mainstream. GDPR (2018), CCPA (2020) and similar laws regulate data handling. Apple's App Tracking Transparency (2021) reshaped mobile advertising.
now.open_questions: How do encrypted backups and 'lawful access' debates resolve? UK Online Safety Act 2023 and EU Chat Control proposals reopen the encryption debate.

items.reflection: Snowden remains in Russia, granted citizenship in 2022. The technical changes his disclosures triggered — encryption by default, certificate transparency, the death of unencrypted email — have outlasted the political moment.

moments.title: Shor's algorithm
moments.body: Shor proves that a quantum computer could factor integers in polynomial time, breaking RSA and most public-key cryptography. At the time no quantum computer existed that could run it on any non-trivial number. The result triggers serious investment in quantum computing research.
moments.takeaway: A theoretical algorithm motivated thirty years of physics-engineering investment, because the consequences for global security were too large to ignore.

moments.title: Sycamore claims quantum supremacy
moments.body: Google's 53-qubit Sycamore processor performs a specific (impractical) sampling task in 200 seconds. Google estimates it would take a classical supercomputer 10,000 years; IBM contests the estimate (2.5 days with the right method). The 'supremacy' claim becomes 'quantum advantage' in subsequent papers.
moments.takeaway: The first claim of computational tasks beyond classical reach was narrow, contested, and a meaningful milestone.

now.title: Quantum computing today
now.body: IBM, Google, IonQ, Quantinuum, PsiQuantum, Atom Computing and others pursue different qubit technologies (superconducting, trapped ion, photonic, neutral atom). Error-correction is the central challenge. NIST has standardised post-quantum cryptography algorithms (2024) in anticipation of cryptographically relevant quantum computers.
now.open_questions: When (if ever) will fault-tolerant quantum computers exist? Estimates range from 5 to 50 years.

items.reflection: Quantum computing is the rare research area where the destination (breaking RSA) was known before the journey was started. Forty years of investment have not produced a useful machine. They have, however, produced enormous progress in physics.

moments.title: SolarWinds breach
moments.body: Discovered in December 2020 by FireEye, the SolarWinds supply-chain attack inserted a backdoor into Orion network management software updates from March 2020. ~18,000 organisations downloaded the compromised update; ~100 were actively exploited, including US Treasury, Commerce, State Department and Microsoft.
moments.takeaway: Software updates — long considered the right thing to do for security — became the attack vector itself. Trust in the supply chain became a first-order security concern.

now.title: Supply chain security today
now.body: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), reproducible builds, signed packages and SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) levels are now serious areas of practice. The XZ Utils backdoor (March 2024), discovered through a 500ms login delay, showed how patient supply-chain attacks on open source can be.
now.open_questions: How can volunteer-maintained open-source dependencies be made resistant to nation-state attackers without burdening maintainers?

items.reflection: The XZ Utils attacker spent two years building trust in the project before introducing the backdoor. Open-source maintainers are now vetting contributors with active intelligence in mind.

moments.title: Agile Manifesto
moments.body: In February 2001, 17 developers — including Kent Beck (Extreme Programming), Martin Fowler, Ward Cunningham, Robert Martin, Jeff Sutherland and Ken Schwaber (Scrum) — meet at a ski resort and produce the Agile Manifesto: four values, twelve principles. 'Individuals and interactions over processes and tools.'
moments.takeaway: A short document by 17 people defined how the global software industry organises work for the next 25 years.

now.title: Software process today
now.body: Agile, Scrum, Kanban and SAFe are standard in most software organisations. The original signatories have mostly become critics of how Agile has been implemented — particularly large enterprise frameworks. DevOps (2009), continuous deployment, and SRE practices (Google, 2003) extended the same ideas to operations.
now.open_questions: Did Agile improve software outcomes or just speed up bad software? Empirical evidence is mixed.

items.reflection: The Manifesto's signatories had vastly different practices. They agreed on values rather than methodology. Most subsequent debate has confused the two.

moments.title: Multics project announced
moments.body: Multics (Multiplexed Information and Computing Service) is announced as a joint project to build a time-sharing operating system supporting hundreds of simultaneous users with reliability comparable to a public utility. The project introduces many concepts that became standard: hierarchical file systems, dynamic linking, segmented memory, security rings.
moments.takeaway: An over-ambitious 1960s research project introduced most of the ideas underlying modern operating systems — including the rings of protection still used in x86 CPUs.

now.title: Multics today
now.body: Bell Labs withdrew in 1969 (Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie went on to write Unix as a reaction). Multics ran on production systems until 2000. Honeywell, the eventual hardware vendor, sold Multics to ~80 customers — modest commercially, vast in influence.
now.open_questions: Why do over-ambitious research projects often produce more lasting ideas than successful commercial products? Multics, Smalltalk, Plan 9 and others follow a pattern.

items.reflection: Unix was conceived partly as 'Multics minus the bits that didn't work'. The name 'Unix' is a pun on 'eunuchs' (castrated Multics) and on 'uni-' (single user, originally). Engineering humour is part of the historical record.

moments.title: MS-DOS ships
moments.body: Microsoft buys 86-DOS from Seattle Computer Products for $50,000, modifies it lightly, and licences it to IBM as PC-DOS for the new IBM 5150. Microsoft retains the right to licence MS-DOS to other vendors. The Compaq clone (1982) opens a massive market. Bill Gates: 'We were lucky that nobody else at IBM thought we were important.'
moments.takeaway: A $50,000 acquisition turned into Microsoft's foundational franchise. Licence terms can be worth orders of magnitude more than product.

now.title: Microsoft today
now.body: Windows runs on ~73% of desktop PCs. Microsoft is now valued at $3+ trillion, transitioning from Windows-first to cloud-first (Azure) and AI (OpenAI partnership, $13bn invested). The transition under Satya Nadella (CEO from 2014) is widely studied as a corporate reinvention.
now.open_questions: Can OpenAI's relationship with Microsoft survive their parallel ambitions? Co-investor and competitor dynamics are complex.

items.reflection: Gary Kildall of Digital Research is sometimes blamed for missing the IBM-DOS deal (he wasn't home when IBM visited). The reality is messier; IBM and Kildall couldn't agree on terms. Sometimes a deal not done shapes an industry more than one done.

moments.title: C with Classes at Bell Labs
moments.body: Stroustrup, a Danish computer scientist, begins extending C with object-oriented features inspired by Simula. The language is renamed C++ in 1983. First commercial release: 1985. C++ supports classes, inheritance, virtual functions, templates and operator overloading. It becomes the dominant language for performance-critical applications.
moments.takeaway: A language designed to add OOP to systems programming became one of the most widely used and most criticised languages of the next 40 years.

now.title: C++ today
now.body: C++ runs browsers (Chromium), databases (MongoDB), game engines (Unreal), high-frequency trading, scientific computing and most operating-system userland. Modern C++ (C++11, 14, 17, 20, 23) is significantly safer than 1990s C++. Rust competes for new systems code; C++ codebase migration is gradual.
now.open_questions: Can C++ remain relevant against memory-safe alternatives? Stroustrup remains active on its standards committee.

items.reflection: Stroustrup: 'Within C++, there is a much smaller and cleaner language struggling to get out.' Few languages have been so simultaneously useful and despised.

moments.title: JavaScript in 10 days
moments.body: Eich writes the first version of JavaScript (originally LiveScript, renamed for marketing reasons to associate with Java) in 10 days in May 1995. The language ships in Netscape Navigator 2.0 in September. ECMAScript standardisation (Ecma International) follows in 1997.
moments.takeaway: The most-used programming language in the world was designed in 10 days under marketing pressure. Many of its quirks reflect that timeline.

moments.title: Node.js
moments.body: Dahl releases Node.js, embedding Google's V8 JavaScript engine on the server with non-blocking I/O. JavaScript becomes a full-stack language. npm (2010) becomes the largest package registry in any language. The frontend/backend language unification is a major industry shift.
moments.takeaway: JavaScript escaped the browser. A single language now runs both ends of most web applications and many desktop apps (Electron).

now.title: JavaScript today
now.body: TypeScript (Microsoft, 2012) adds static types to JavaScript and is now the default for new web projects. React (Facebook 2013), Vue (2014), Angular (Google) compete for frontend mindshare. Deno (2018, by Ryan Dahl as a Node successor) and Bun (2022) compete with Node.
now.open_questions: Will WebAssembly replace JavaScript for performance-sensitive web code? Adoption is gradual.

items.reflection: Eich was forced to step down as Mozilla CEO in 2014 over personal political donations. The architect of the web's most-used language was removed from leading its most-used browser by the community he built. Open source has political dimensions.

moments.title: Facebook launched at Harvard
moments.body: TheFacebook launches on 4 February 2004 at Harvard. Within a month, half of Harvard undergraduates have profiles. It expands to other Ivy League universities, then all US colleges (2005), then global (2006). News Feed (2006) is initially hated by users; the iPhone (2007) and the mobile app dominate engagement.
moments.takeaway: A college-only social network reached 3 billion monthly active users within 20 years. The transformation of how humans talk to each other happened within a single career.

moments.title: YouTube launches and is acquired
moments.who: Steve Chen, Chad Hurley, Jawed Karim; Google
moments.body: YouTube launches in February 2005 from an apartment in San Mateo. The first video, 'Me at the zoo' (23 April 2005, 19 seconds), is uploaded by Karim. Google acquires YouTube in October 2006 for $1.65 billion in stock. Now over 500 hours of video are uploaded every minute.
moments.takeaway: A site for sharing home videos became the world's largest online video platform within 18 months.

now.title: Social media today
now.body: TikTok (ByteDance, 2016 global) overtook Facebook and YouTube for time-spent among younger users. EU Digital Services Act (2022) and content moderation legal debates shape platform behaviour. The 2024 US TikTok ban legislation and 2025 partial divestment showed how platform geopolitics evolved. Misinformation, polarisation and youth mental-health concerns are ongoing.
now.open_questions: Can platforms be regulated for safety while preserving speech and innovation? Different jurisdictions are settling at very different points.

items.reflection: Facebook's 'move fast and break things' motto was abandoned in 2014. The things it broke included some elements of democratic discourse. The cost of growth-at-all-costs cultures is now better understood.

moments.title: GeForce 256 GPU
moments.body: Nvidia ships the GeForce 256 in October 1999, marketing it as 'the world's first GPU' (graphics processing unit). It performs transformation and lighting on the card, offloading the CPU. Subsequent generations add programmable shaders. Buoyed by gaming demand, GPUs become massively parallel computing engines.
moments.takeaway: A gaming graphics chip evolved into the substrate of modern AI. Nvidia was a games company for two decades before becoming an AI infrastructure company.

moments.title: CUDA launches
moments.body: Nvidia releases CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture), letting general-purpose programs run on GPUs in C. Within years, scientific computing, oil-and-gas modelling, finance and (most consequentially) machine learning adopt CUDA. The 2012 AlexNet paper used CUDA on GTX 580 GPUs.
moments.takeaway: A toolkit released to keep gamers buying upgrades enabled the deep-learning revolution five years later.

now.title: GPUs and AI today
now.body: Nvidia's market cap exceeded $3 trillion in 2024. H100 and B100 GPUs are the substrate of large language model training. AMD's MI300 and Google TPUs compete. Geopolitics of chip supply (US export controls on advanced GPUs to China since 2022) shape the AI landscape. CUDA remains a software moat for Nvidia.
now.open_questions: Can AI workloads diversify across chip vendors? Or will Nvidia's CUDA lock-in persist?

items.reflection: Jensen Huang founded Nvidia in 1993 at Denny's in San Jose. The CEO of one of the world's most valuable companies still wears the same black leather jacket to keynotes. Founder-led tech continuity over decades remains a striking pattern.

moments.title: Go at Google
moments.who: Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike, Ken Thompson, Google
moments.body: Three engineers at Google design Go (started 2007, open-sourced November 2009) as a response to the complexity of C++ and the latency of waiting for compile times. Built-in concurrency via goroutines, garbage collection, simple syntax, fast compilation. Docker (2013) and Kubernetes (2014) are both written in Go.
moments.takeaway: A modern language designed by Unix veterans became the foundation of cloud-native infrastructure within five years.

moments.title: Rust 1.0
moments.body: Rust began as Hoare's personal project in 2006, was sponsored by Mozilla from 2009, and reached 1.0 in May 2015. Memory safety without garbage collection (via ownership and borrowing) addresses a long-standing systems-programming gap. Linux kernel accepted Rust code from 2022; Windows and Android are adding Rust components.
moments.takeaway: A new systems language without a runtime overhead became serious enough for kernel use within a decade.

now.title: Modern languages today
now.body: Go dominates cloud infrastructure. Rust is the default new-systems language at many major companies. Swift (Apple, 2014), Kotlin (JetBrains, 2011) and TypeScript reshaped Apple, Android and web development. The 2022 ONCD report and 2024 White House guidance recommended migration from memory-unsafe languages.
now.open_questions: Can existing C/C++ codebases be migrated to memory-safe languages at scale? Linux kernel's Rust experiment is the leading test.

items.reflection: Both Go and Rust were developed inside large companies (Google, Mozilla) with full-time language design teams. Modern language design is increasingly a corporate function rather than an academic one.

moments.title: Docker open-sourced
moments.body: Docker is unveiled at PyCon on 15 March 2013. It uses Linux namespaces and cgroups (existing kernel features) to wrap applications in portable containers. Within three years, container deployment becomes industry standard. dotCloud renames to Docker Inc.
moments.takeaway: Docker did not invent containers (LXC, BSD jails predate it) — it productised them with a great developer experience. Tool design matters as much as core technology.

moments.title: Kubernetes released
